title: The throat-and-dot family: ج ح خ / د ذ
objectives: Student can identify and pronounce ج, ح, خ, د, ذ in isolation on sight.
Student can consistently distinguish ح (heavy, mid-throat) from خ (upper-throat) and from ه (light — taught later, flagged now as "the sound you'll meet later that's NOT this").
Student can distinguish د (plain "d") from ذ (voiced "th" as in "this").

slides.heading: Lesson 1.2 — The throat-and-dot family: ج ح خ / د ذ
Quick recap — last lesson's four letters

audio.cue: ا: an open, unobstructed sound from deep in the chest cavity — no closure anywhere, just a clear open vowel
lips fully together
tongue-tip on gum ridge
tongue between teeth

slides.heading: The throat has three zones
body: The throat divides into three zones: deep (hamza — a glottal-stop mark — and ه, both met later), mid (ع/ح — ع met later), upper (غ/خ — غ met later)
Two of today's five letters are throat letters — often the single most error-prone family in the whole alphabet for learners coming from your language background
Today we meet the mid-zone ح and the upper-zone خ

slides.makhraj: middle of the tongue against the roof of the mouth
notes: Shape-family with ح and خ — ج has one dot BELOW
Sound: a soft "j" affricate (Husary/Muallim standard) — not a hard "g" or "zh"

audio.cue: ح: a strong, breathy, unvoiced friction from the middle of the throat — like fogging a mirror from deep in the throat, no English equivalent

notes: Same body-family as ج/خ — ح has NO dot
A strong, unvoiced, breathy throat friction — "like fogging a mirror from mid-throat"
No equivalent phoneme exists in English, Turkish, Uzbek, Persian, or Urdu

audio.cue: خ: a rasping fricative from the upper throat/back of the tongue against the soft palate — a genuine back-of-throat 'kh', not softened

slides.makhraj: upper throat / back of tongue against the soft palate
notes: Same body-family as ج/ح — خ has one dot ABOVE
Close to the "kh" sound Uzbek already has in words like xalq — you likely can say this one already; just keep it a genuine back-of-throat fricative, not softened

slides.heading: ح vs خ vs ه — the #1 mistake in the alphabet
slides.instructions: Listen to all three back to back (ه is only a preview here — it's formally taught in Lesson 1.6), then point to which one you heard.

audio.cue: ح: a strong, breathy, unvoiced friction from the middle of the throat — like fogging a mirror from deep in the throat, no English equivalent
خ: a rasping fricative from the upper throat/back of the tongue against the soft palate — a genuine back-of-throat 'kh', not softened
ه: a light, breathy release from the throat — softer and further back than an English 'h', much gentler than ح
د: tongue-tip taps the upper gum ridge firmly — a plain, crisp 'd'

slides.makhraj: tip of tongue against the upper gum ridge
notes: Shape-family with ذ — same body, د has NO dot

audio.cue: ذ: tongue-tip between the teeth, same point as ث but VOICED — 'th' as in 'this', never a 'z'

slides.makhraj: tip of tongue between the teeth (same point as ث, but voiced)
notes: Shape-family with د — same body, ذ has one dot ABOVE
Voiced "th" as in "this" — NOT a "z"; documented as a Persian/Turkish/Urdu-speaker collapse pattern

slides.heading: د vs ذ — minimal-pair listening
slides.instructions: Listen for either د or ذ, then point to which glyph you heard.

audio.cue: د: tongue-tip taps the upper gum ridge firmly — a plain, crisp 'd'
ذ: tongue-tip between the teeth, same point as ث but VOICED — 'th' as in 'this', never a 'z'

Cumulative shuffle drill of all 9 letters learned so far, reviewing lesson 1.1's letters too (ا ب ت ث ج ح خ د ذ)

dailyChecklist: Write today's letters (ج ح خ د ذ) 4 rows each in your notebook, saying the name and sound aloud as you write
Flashcard round ×3 (ج ح خ د ذ, mixed order)

script: Open with a cold-call recap of ا ب ت ث before introducing today's family.
Explain the three throat zones in plain English before naming ج ح خ ذ د individually.
Model ح and خ 3× each before asking the student to imitate — correct the FIRST wrong repetition, not the third.
Self-check your own ح/خ against the linked Arabic101 Makharij videos before the lesson — this is the single lesson to audition hardest.
Budget the most correction time of the lesson on ح vs خ vs ه, per the sourced research's #1-mistake flag.
listenFor: ح substituted with خ or with the light ه — flagged in the sourced research as "the single most-cited non-Arab error" (teaching-mistakes-assessment.md A.1); no equivalent phoneme exists in English, Turkish, Uzbek, Persian, or Urdu. Give this the most correction time in the lesson.
خ losing its heaviness, flattened toward the student's L1 "x" sound (A.1) — watch that it stays a genuine back-of-throat fricative, not a softened palatal one.
ج over- or under-affricated (some traditions say "zh" or hard "g" — this course follows the Husary/Muallim standard soft-j articulation; watch for L1-transfer toward a hard "g").

ذ collapsing toward a plain "z" — explicitly documented as a Persian/Turkish/Urdu-speaker pattern (A.3: "the emphatic sounds become just another way to say 'Z' in these languages") and directly relevant to an Uzbek-background student; confirm this specific substitution against the student's actual speech in this lesson, don't assume.
د/ذ merged into a single sound generally.
teacherNotes.homework: In the student's notebook: each new letter (ج ح خ د ذ) written 4 full rows, saying its name and sound aloud while writing, then memorized; daily 2-minute throat warm-up (ح, خ, ه(anticipatory) 5× each, self-recorded if possible and compared against the linked Arabic101 videos); cumulative shuffle of all 9 letters learned so far. No printed sheets.
